class.name: NetwSpawnPlanner
class.brief_description: Turns the committed interest matrix into what each peer is owed: which routes to spawn, retain or despawn.
class.description: Deciding and doing are kept separate on purpose. Both methods are pure functions of their arguments, so what a peer is sent never depends on the order anything happened to be iterated in. [method reconcile] reads rows in parent-before-child order for one pass and applies that ordering twice, forward and backward, because a gain must be planned parent before child (a peer that receives a child before its parent has nowhere to put it) and a loss must be planned child before parent, the same reason read backwards. A row's parent must therefore already be decided before the row itself is, which is why [method ancestry_order] exists: it is the book order [method reconcile] requires its rows delivered in.

method.name: ancestry_order
method.description: Answers [param routes] with every route after its parent. [param parents] maps a route to its parent route, or to [code]0[/code] where it anchors nothing. Arm order is not ancestry order, and the gap is not rare: a reparent moves an entity under a parent armed after it, so a clamp that read a parent's verdict before this reorders it would leave the mover permanently unspawnable. Tree ancestry cannot cycle, so a pass that places nothing means the remaining anchors are mid-move; those routes are appended in arm order rather than dropped, because a route missing from the answer is never sent to anyone.

method.name: reconcile
method.description: Plans [param peers] against [param rows], which arrive in parent-before-child book order (see [method ancestry_order]). A row whose parent is not in [param rows] is unclamped. Each row is [code]{route, parent_route, recipients, local_desired, leave}[/code]. [code]local_desired[/code] is what the interest layer decided about that row alone, per peer; a child is owed a route only where its parent is too, and clamping [code]local_desired[/code] against the parent's own answer, combined with the parent-before-child and child-before-parent read orders, is what makes those two orderings sufficient with no third pass. [code]leave[/code] maps a peer to a [code]{despawn, custom}[/code] decision this plane CARRIES rather than interprets: it decides only WHETHER a peer keeps a route it is no longer owed, and [code]custom[/code] is opaque all the way through to whichever layer gave it meaning. Each operation is [code]{action, route, peer}[/code], plus [code]{decision, forced}[/code] whenever [code]action[/code] is not a spawn. A spawn carries no leave policy, because nothing is being left. [code]forced[/code] is true when a parent's own despawn forced this operation, so the row's own decision lost to it.
